text:
Rowan University recently adopted a new Artificial Intelligence (AI) Policy that establishes rules around how institutional data may be used in tools like ChatGPT.
The policy, which was jointly issued by the Division of Information Resources & Technology and the Office of the Provost, states:
1	Only Rowan data classified as public may be used in non-approved AI tools. 
2	Data of any classification type other than public may only be used in approved AI tools.


Appropriate and acceptable use of G-AI tools includes the following:
•	Research or learn something new, and/or help your own learning and understanding of any topic.
•	Idea brainstorming for projects, proposals, discussion points, etc.
•	Literature searches to suggest papers or summarize academic content; however, literature review and final citations must always be your synthesis of the reviewed content, and be confirmed from verifiable and reputable sources (e.g., Google Scholar, IEEE, arXiv).
•	For starting or creating a general/routine structure for coding, and/or debugging your code, so long as the substantial/vast majority (75% or higher, not counting the documentation part) of the code is yours, and that *you* understand, test, and document the code entirely and thoroughly. You will be asked to explain your code and demonstrate your understanding, and thereby prove that it is your own work. • Routine proof-reading for correcting grammar, typos, clarifying or correcting sentences, so long as the original sentences are yours. • Generating non-technical figures to be used as concept illustrations (subject to course-specific permissions - check with the course instructor) • Any assignment or exercise where the instructor specifically and explicitly asks you to use an AI tool for a specific task or purpose that is aligned with course objectives and/or outcomes. Use of G-AI tools for any of the following is inappropriate and not allowed: The following is a set of examples and not an exhaustive list. Some overlap and repetition among the following items is deliberate and intended for reinforcement. If you are unsure whether a particular G-AI use case is appropriate, please reach out to your course professor. • Any use of a G-AI tool that is not properly and thoroughly cited (see below for guidelines on how to cite AI-generated content). • Solving or answering any questions in any graded assignment, quiz, exam, or report. • Analyzing data, drawing conclusions based on experiments or data analysis to be used in any graded assignment. • Answering any essay-type questions (other than for language clarification as indicated above) in any graded assignment, quiz, exam, or report. • Determining impact factors, ethical and professional considerations for any design-related course (including Embedded Systems, Engineering Clinics, Professionalism & Consulting, Frontiers in Engineering) that asks you to articulate your design decisions, professional judgment, and ethical discussions in consideration of impact factors. • Code or code fragments that exceed 25% of the total script for any programming assignment or any project that requires you to develop code. If the instructor provides you with a base code to modify or to add to, then the modifications or additions cannot be AI-generated and must all be your work. • Uploading class/course material, lecture notes to any unauthorized G-AI tool (e.g., ChatGPT and others), or online learning platform (including Chegg, CourseHero, and other similar platforms). • Mathematical derivations submitted as part of a graded assignment, quiz, exam, or report. • Algorithm design submitted as part of a graded assignment, quiz, exam, or report. • Using AI to generate any part or section of a lab report, project report, or any other submission. For example, uploading raw data, results, or incomplete notes into AI to generate a report is not permitted. • Using AI to interpret, process, or analyze results from simulations. Either case is a form of academic integrity violation that will not be tolerated and will be reported to the Provost’s Office in accordance with Rowan University's Academic Integrity Policy. 2 Lecture notes made available to you are the intellectual property of the course developer/instructor. Rowan University recently adopted a new Artificial Intelligence (AI) Policy that establishes rules around how institutional data may be used in tools like ChatGPT.
The policy, which was jointly issued by the Division of Information Resources & Technology and the Office of the Provost, states:
1	Only Rowan data classified as public may be used in non-approved AI tools. 
2	Data of any classification type other than public may only be used in approved AI tools.


Appropriate and acceptable use of G-AI tools includes the following:
•	Research or learn something new, and/or help your own learning and understanding of any topic.
•	Idea brainstorming for projects, proposals, discussion points, etc.
•	Literature searches to suggest papers or summarize academic content; however, literature review and final citations must always be your synthesis of the reviewed content, and be confirmed from verifiable and reputable sources (e.g., Google Scholar, IEEE, arXiv).
•	For starting or creating a general/routine structure for coding, and/or debugging your code, so long as the substantial/vast majority (75% or higher, not counting the documentation part) of the code is yours, and that *you* understand, test, and document the code entirely and thoroughly. You will be asked to explain your code and demonstrate your understanding, and thereby prove that it is your own work.
•	Routine proof-reading for correcting grammar, typos, clarifying or correcting sentences, so long as the original sentences are yours.
•	Generating non-technical figures to be used as concept illustrations (subject to course-specific permissions - check with the course instructor)
•	Any assignment or exercise where the instructor specifically and explicitly asks you to use an AI tool for a specific task or purpose that is aligned with course objectives and/or outcomes.
Use of G-AI tools for any of the following is inappropriate and not allowed:
The following is a set of examples and not an exhaustive list. Some overlap and repetition among the following items is deliberate and intended for reinforcement. If you are unsure whether a particular G-AI use case is appropriate, please reach out to your course professor.
•	Any use of a G-AI tool that is not properly and thoroughly cited (see below for guidelines on how to cite AI-generated content).
•	Solving or answering any questions in any graded assignment, quiz, exam, or report.
•	Analyzing data, drawing conclusions based on experiments or data analysis to be used in any graded assignment.
•	Answering any essay-type questions (other than for language clarification as indicated above) in any graded assignment, quiz, exam, or report.
•	Determining impact factors, ethical and professional considerations for any design-related course (including Embedded Systems, Engineering Clinics, Professionalism & Consulting, Frontiers in Engineering) that asks you to articulate your design decisions, professional judgment, and ethical discussions in consideration of impact factors. 
•	Code or code fragments that exceed 25% of the total script for any programming assignment or any project that requires you to develop code. If the instructor provides you with a base code to modify or to add to, then the modifications or additions cannot be AI-generated and must all be your work.
•	Uploading class/course material, lecture notes to any unauthorized G-AI tool (e.g., ChatGPT and others), or online learning platform (including Chegg, CourseHero, and other similar platforms).
•	Mathematical derivations submitted as part of a graded assignment, quiz, exam, or report.
•	Algorithm design submitted as part of a graded assignment, quiz, exam, or report.
•	Using AI to generate any part or section of a lab report, project report, or any other submission. For example, uploading raw data, results, or incomplete notes into AI to generate a report is not permitted.
•	Using AI to interpret, process, or analyze results from simulations.
It is worth noting that:
1	Pretending or presenting any content as if it is yours that is, in fact, generated by others (including Gen AI) is plagiarism. Paraphrasing or rewording the borrowed content to hide its original source is not only plagiarism, but also academic dishonesty. Either case is a form of academic integrity violation that will not be tolerated and will be reported to the Provost’s Office in accordance with Rowan University's Academic Integrity Policy.
2	Lecture notes made available to you are the intellectual property of the course developer/instructor. These lecture notes and materials are copyrighted and protected by copyright law, regardless of whether a copyright notice is visible (as is the case for any work of authorship under US law). When provided to you (such as on Canvas), you are merely given the very limited right to use them for your own personal learning. Therefore, uploading any course content to any online portal, including online learning platforms such as Course Hero, Chegg, etc., or any Gen AI platforms (such as ChatGPT, CoPilot, Gemini, etc.) is illegal and strictly prohibited. If detected, it will be reported as an Academic Integrity Violation at Level 3 or Level 4. The instructor (or content owner) may also independently take legal action against you under Copyright Law.  Simply stated: do not upload any course materials/content to any unauthorized site without the express written permission of the instructor/copyright holder.

text:
Rowan University recently adopted a new Artificial Intelligence (AI) Policy that establishes rules around how institutional data may be used in tools like ChatGPT.
The policy, which was jointly issued by the Division of Information Resources & Technology and the Office of the Provost, states:
1	Only Rowan data classified as public may be used in non-approved AI tools. 
2	Data of any classification type other than public may only be used in approved AI tools.


Appropriate and acceptable use of G-AI tools includes the following:
•	Research or learn something new, and/or help your own learning and understanding of any topic.
•	Idea brainstorming for projects, proposals, discussion points, etc.
•	Literature searches to suggest papers or summarize academic content; however, literature review and final citations must always be your synthesis of the reviewed content, and be confirmed from verifiable and reputable sources (e.g., Google Scholar, IEEE, arXiv).
•	For starting or creating a general/routine structure for coding, and/or debugging your code, so long as the substantial/vast majority (75% or higher, not counting the documentation part) of the code is yours, and that *you* understand, test, and document the code entirely and thoroughly. You will be asked to explain your code and demonstrate your understanding, and thereby prove that it is your own work.
•	Routine proof-reading for correcting grammar, typos, clarifying or correcting sentences, so long as the original sentences are yours.
•	Generating non-technical figures to be used as concept illustrations (subject to course-specific permissions - check with the course instructor)
•	Any assignment or exercise where the instructor specifically and explicitly asks you to use an AI tool for a specific task or purpose that is aligned with course objectives and/or outcomes.
Use of G-AI tools for any of the following is inappropriate and not allowed:
The following is a set of examples and not an exhaustive list. Some overlap and repetition among the following items is deliberate and intended for reinforcement. If you are unsure whether a particular G-AI use case is appropriate, please reach out to your course professor.
•	Any use of a G-AI tool that is not properly and thoroughly cited (see below for guidelines on how to cite AI-generated content).
•	Solving or answering any questions in any graded assignment, quiz, exam, or report.
•	Analyzing data, drawing conclusions based on experiments or data analysis to be used in any graded assignment.
•	Answering any essay-type questions (other than for language clarification as indicated above) in any graded assignment, quiz, exam, or report.
•	Determining impact factors, ethical and professional considerations for any design-related course (including Embedded Systems, Engineering Clinics, Professionalism & Consulting, Frontiers in Engineering) that asks you to articulate your design decisions, professional judgment, and ethical discussions in consideration of impact factors. 
•	Code or code fragments that exceed 25% of the total script for any programming assignment or any project that requires you to develop code. If the instructor provides you with a base code to modify or to add to, then the modifications or additions cannot be AI-generated and must all be your work.
•	Uploading class/course material, lecture notes to any unauthorized G-AI tool (e.g., ChatGPT and others), or online learning platform (including Chegg, CourseHero, and other similar platforms).
•	Mathematical derivations submitted as part of a graded assignment, quiz, exam, or report.
•	Algorithm design submitted as part of a graded assignment, quiz, exam, or report.
•	Using AI to generate any part or section of a lab report, project report, or any other submission. For example, uploading raw data, results, or incomplete notes into AI to generate a report is not permitted.
•	Using AI to interpret, process, or analyze results from simulations.
It is worth noting that:
1	Pretending or presenting any content as if it is yours that is, in fact, generated by others (including Gen AI) is plagiarism. Paraphrasing or rewording the borrowed content to hide its original source is not only plagiarism, but also academic dishonesty. Either case is a form of academic integrity violation that will not be tolerated and will be reported to the Provost’s Office in accordance with Rowan University's Academic Integrity Policy.
2	Lecture notes made available to you are the intellectual property of the course developer/instructor. These lecture notes and materials are copyrighted and protected by copyright law, regardless of whether a copyright notice is visible (as is the case for any work of authorship under US law). When provided to you (such as on Canvas), you are merely given the very limited right to use them for your own personal learning. Therefore, uploading any course content to any online portal, including online learning platforms such as Course Hero, Chegg, etc., or any Gen AI platforms (such as ChatGPT, CoPilot, Gemini, etc.) is illegal and strictly prohibited. If detected, it will be reported as an Academic Integrity Violation at Level 3 or Level 4. The instructor (or content owner) may also independently take legal action against you under Copyright Law.  Simply stated: do not upload any course materials/content to any unauthorized site without the express written permission of the instructor/copyright holder.
Citing G-AI tools:
In all cases, the specific use of a G-AI tool must be properly and completely cited as follows:
•	Citing routine use of a built-in G-AI tool to correct individual errors for grammar, typos, clarification, etc., use the following format with only one citation for the entire document.
<Company name)>, <Name of the tool>. Accessed on <date in which you          used the tool>, Model or Version: <model or version used>, <descriptor>. Available at:        <link to the main page for the tool>. Context: provide a brief description of the use.
•	Example 1: Grammarly Inc, Grammarly. Accessed on 15 June 2025, Version: 14.1232.0 (browser), large language model-based writing assistant integrated into Word. Available at:  https://www.grammarly.com. Context: used for routine grammar /typo correction.
◦	Example 2: Google, Gemini. Accessed on 20 July 2025, Model: Gemini 2.0 Flash, large language model-based writing assistant integrated into Google Docs. Available at: https://gemini.google.com/app. Context: used for routine correction for grammar and typos, and obtaining a more concise writing.
•	For all other and more substantial uses of G-AI tools, use the following format, and include a separate citation for each use. If you are using up to three prompts, include all. For longer conversations, include the first, second, and last prompt with ellipses (...) in between.  For additional clarification, when needed, provide context. text:
Rowan University recently adopted a new Artificial Intelligence (AI) Policy that establishes rules around how institutional data may be used in tools like ChatGPT.
The policy, which was jointly issued by the Division of Information Resources & Technology and the Office of the Provost, states:
1	Only Rowan data classified as public may be used in non-approved AI tools. 
2	Data of any classification type other than public may only be used in approved AI tools.


Appropriate and acceptable use of G-AI tools includes the following:
•	Research or learn something new, and/or help your own learning and understanding of any topic.
•	Idea brainstorming for projects, proposals, discussion points, etc.
•	Literature searches to suggest papers or summarize academic content; however, literature review and final citations must always be your synthesis of the reviewed content, and be confirmed from verifiable and reputable sources (e.g., Google Scholar, IEEE, arXiv).
•	For starting or creating a general/routine structure for coding, and/or debugging your code, so long as the substantial/vast majority (75% or higher, not counting the documentation part) of the code is yours, and that *you* understand, test, and document the code entirely and thoroughly. You will be asked to explain your code and demonstrate your understanding, and thereby prove that it is your own work.
•	Routine proof-reading for correcting grammar, typos, clarifying or correcting sentences, so long as the original sentences are yours.
•	Generating non-technical figures to be used as concept illustrations (subject to course-specific permissions - check with the course instructor)
•	Any assignment or exercise where the instructor specifically and explicitly asks you to use an AI tool for a specific task or purpose that is aligned with course objectives and/or outcomes.
Use of G-AI tools for any of the following is inappropriate and not allowed:
The following is a set of examples and not an exhaustive list. Some overlap and repetition among the following items is deliberate and intended for reinforcement. If you are unsure whether a particular G-AI use case is appropriate, please reach out to your course professor.
•	Any use of a G-AI tool that is not properly and thoroughly cited (see below for guidelines on how to cite AI-generated content).
•	Solving or answering any questions in any graded assignment, quiz, exam, or report.
•	Analyzing data, drawing conclusions based on experiments or data analysis to be used in any graded assignment.
•	Answering any essay-type questions (other than for language clarification as indicated above) in any graded assignment, quiz, exam, or report.
•	Determining impact factors, ethical and professional considerations for any design-related course (including Embedded Systems, Engineering Clinics, Professionalism & Consulting, Frontiers in Engineering) that asks you to articulate your design decisions, professional judgment, and ethical discussions in consideration of impact factors. 
•	Code or code fragments that exceed 25% of the total script for any programming assignment or any project that requires you to develop code. If the instructor provides you with a base code to modify or to add to, then the modifications or additions cannot be AI-generated and must all be your work.
•	Uploading class/course material, lecture notes to any unauthorized G-AI tool (e.g., ChatGPT and others), or online learning platform (including Chegg, CourseHero, and other similar platforms).
•	Mathematical derivations submitted as part of a graded assignment, quiz, exam, or report.
•	Algorithm design submitted as part of a graded assignment, quiz, exam, or report.
•	Using AI to generate any part or section of a lab report, project report, or any other submission. For example, uploading raw data, results, or incomplete notes into AI to generate a report is not permitted.
•	Using AI to interpret, process, or analyze results from simulations.
It is worth noting that:
1	Pretending or presenting any content as if it is yours that is, in fact, generated by others (including Gen AI) is plagiarism. Paraphrasing or rewording the borrowed content to hide its original source is not only plagiarism, but also academic dishonesty. Either case is a form of academic integrity violation that will not be tolerated and will be reported to the Provost’s Office in accordance with Rowan University's Academic Integrity Policy.
2	Lecture notes made available to you are the intellectual property of the course developer/instructor. These lecture notes and materials are copyrighted and protected by copyright law, regardless of whether a copyright notice is visible (as is the case for any work of authorship under US law). When provided to you (such as on Canvas), you are merely given the very limited right to use them for your own personal learning. Therefore, uploading any course content to any online portal, including online learning platforms such as Course Hero, Chegg, etc., or any Gen AI platforms (such as ChatGPT, CoPilot, Gemini, etc.) is illegal and strictly prohibited. If detected, it will be reported as an Academic Integrity Violation at Level 3 or Level 4. The instructor (or content owner) may also independently take legal action against you under Copyright Law.  Simply stated: do not upload any course materials/content to any unauthorized site without the express written permission of the instructor/copyright holder.
Citing G-AI tools:
In all cases, the specific use of a G-AI tool must be properly and completely cited as follows:
•	Citing routine use of a built-in G-AI tool to correct individual errors for grammar, typos, clarification, etc., use the following format with only one citation for the entire document.

text:
Rowan University recently adopted a new Artificial Intelligence (AI) Policy that establishes rules around how institutional data may be used in tools like ChatGPT.
The policy, which was jointly issued by the Division of Information Resources & Technology and the Office of the Provost, states:
1	Only Rowan data classified as public may be used in non-approved AI tools. 
2	Data of any classification type other than public may only be used in approved AI tools.


Appropriate and acceptable use of G-AI tools includes the following:
•	Research or learn something new, and/or help your own learning and understanding of any topic.
•	Idea brainstorming for projects, proposals, discussion points, etc.
•	Literature searches to suggest papers or summarize academic content; however, literature review and final citations must always be your synthesis of the reviewed content, and be confirmed from verifiable and reputable sources (e.g., Google Scholar, IEEE, arXiv).
•	For starting or creating a general/routine structure for coding, and/or debugging your code, so long as the substantial/vast majority (75% or higher, not counting the documentation part) of the code is yours, and that *you* understand, test, and document the code entirely and thoroughly. You will be asked to explain your code and demonstrate your understanding, and thereby prove that it is your own work.
•	Routine proof-reading for correcting grammar, typos, clarifying or correcting sentences, so long as the original sentences are yours.
•	Generating non-technical figures to be used as concept illustrations (subject to course-specific permissions - check with the course instructor)
•	Any assignment or exercise where the instructor specifically and explicitly asks you to use an AI tool for a specific task or purpose that is aligned with course objectives and/or outcomes.
Use of G-AI tools for any of the following is inappropriate and not allowed:
The following is a set of examples and not an exhaustive list. Some overlap and repetition among the following items is deliberate and intended for reinforcement. If you are unsure whether a particular G-AI use case is appropriate, please reach out to your course professor.
•	Any use of a G-AI tool that is not properly and thoroughly cited (see below for guidelines on how to cite AI-generated content).
•	Solving or answering any questions in any graded assignment, quiz, exam, or report.
•	Analyzing data, drawing conclusions based on experiments or data analysis to be used in any graded assignment.
•	Answering any essay-type questions (other than for language clarification as indicated above) in any graded assignment, quiz, exam, or report.
•	Determining impact factors, ethical and professional considerations for any design-related course (including Embedded Systems, Engineering Clinics, Professionalism & Consulting, Frontiers in Engineering) that asks you to articulate your design decisions, professional judgment, and ethical discussions in consideration of impact factors. 
•	Code or code fragments that exceed 25% of the total script for any programming assignment or any project that requires you to develop code. If the instructor provides you with a base code to modify or to add to, then the modifications or additions cannot be AI-generated and must all be your work.
•	Uploading class/course material, lecture notes to any unauthorized G-AI tool (e.g., ChatGPT and others), or online learning platform (including Chegg, CourseHero, and other similar platforms).
•	Mathematical derivations submitted as part of a graded assignment, quiz, exam, or report.
•	Algorithm design submitted as part of a graded assignment, quiz, exam, or report.
•	Using AI to generate any part or section of a lab report, project report, or any other submission. For example, uploading raw data, results, or incomplete notes into AI to generate a report is not permitted.
•	Using AI to interpret, process, or analyze results from simulations.
It is worth noting that:
1	Pretending or presenting any content as if it is yours that is, in fact, generated by others (including Gen AI) is plagiarism. Paraphrasing or rewording the borrowed content to hide its original source is not only plagiarism, but also academic dishonesty. Either case is a form of academic integrity violation that will not be tolerated and will be reported to the Provost’s Office in accordance with Rowan University's Academic Integrity Policy.
2	Lecture notes made available to you are the intellectual property of the course developer/instructor. These lecture notes and materials are copyrighted and protected by copyright law, regardless of whether a copyright notice is visible (as is the case for any work of authorship under US law). When provided to you (such as on Canvas), you are merely given the very limited right to use them for your own personal learning. Therefore, uploading any course content to any online portal, including online learning platforms such as Course Hero, Chegg, etc., or any Gen AI platforms (such as ChatGPT, CoPilot, Gemini, etc.) is illegal and strictly prohibited. text:
Rowan University recently adopted a new Artificial Intelligence (AI) Policy that establishes rules around how institutional data may be used in tools like ChatGPT.
The policy, which was jointly issued by the Division of Information Resources & Technology and the Office of the Provost, states:
1	Only Rowan data classified as public may be used in non-approved AI tools. 
2	Data of any classification type other than public may only be used in approved AI tools.


Appropriate and acceptable use of G-AI tools includes the following:
•	Research or learn something new, and/or help your own learning and understanding of any topic.
•	Idea brainstorming for projects, proposals, discussion points, etc.
•	Literature searches to suggest papers or summarize academic content; however, literature review and final citations must always be your synthesis of the reviewed content, and be confirmed from verifiable and reputable sources (e.g., Google Scholar, IEEE, arXiv).
•	For starting or creating a general/routine structure for coding, and/or debugging your code, so long as the substantial/vast majority (75% or higher, not counting the documentation part) of the code is yours, and that *you* understand, test, and document the code entirely and thoroughly. You will be asked to explain your code and demonstrate your understanding, and thereby prove that it is your own work.
•	Routine proof-reading for correcting grammar, typos, clarifying or correcting sentences, so long as the original sentences are yours.
•	Generating non-technical figures to be used as concept illustrations (subject to course-specific permissions - check with the course instructor)
•	Any assignment or exercise where the instructor specifically and explicitly asks you to use an AI tool for a specific task or purpose that is aligned with course objectives and/or outcomes.
Use of G-AI tools for any of the following is inappropriate and not allowed:
The following is a set of examples and not an exhaustive list. Some overlap and repetition among the following items is deliberate and intended for reinforcement. If you are unsure whether a particular G-AI use case is appropriate, please reach out to your course professor.
•	Any use of a G-AI tool that is not properly and thoroughly cited (see below for guidelines on how to cite AI-generated content).
•	Solving or answering any questions in any graded assignment, quiz, exam, or report.
•	Analyzing data, drawing conclusions based on experiments or data analysis to be used in any graded assignment.
•	Answering any essay-type questions (other than for language clarification as indicated above) in any graded assignment, quiz, exam, or report.
•	Determining impact factors, ethical and professional considerations for any design-related course (including Embedded Systems, Engineering Clinics, Professionalism & Consulting, Frontiers in Engineering) that asks you to articulate your design decisions, professional judgment, and ethical discussions in consideration of impact factors. 
•	Code or code fragments that exceed 25% of the total script for any programming assignment or any project that requires you to develop code. If the instructor provides you with a base code to modify or to add to, then the modifications or additions cannot be AI-generated and must all be your work.
•	Uploading class/course material, lecture notes to any unauthorized G-AI tool (e.g., ChatGPT and others), or online learning platform (including Chegg, CourseHero, and other similar platforms).
•	Mathematical derivations submitted as part of a graded assignment, quiz, exam, or report.
•	Algorithm design submitted as part of a graded assignment, quiz, exam, or report.
•	Using AI to generate any part or section of a lab report, project report, or any other submission. For example, uploading raw data, results, or incomplete notes into AI to generate a report is not permitted.
•	Using AI to interpret, process, or analyze results from simulations.
It is worth noting that:
1	Pretending or presenting any content as if it is yours that is, in fact, generated by others (including Gen AI) is plagiarism. Paraphrasing or rewording the borrowed content to hide its original source is not only plagiarism, but also academic dishonesty. Either case is a form of academic integrity violation that will not be tolerated and will be reported to the Provost’s Office in accordance with Rowan University's Academic Integrity Policy.
2	Lecture notes made available to you are the intellectual property of the course developer/instructor. These lecture notes and materials are copyrighted and protected by copyright law, regardless of whether a copyright notice is visible (as is the case for any work of authorship under US law). When provided to you (such as on Canvas), you are merely given the very limited right to use them for your own personal learning. Therefore, uploading any course content to any online portal, including online learning platforms such as Course Hero, Chegg, etc., or any Gen AI platforms (such as ChatGPT, CoPilot, Gemini, etc.) is illegal and strictly prohibited. If detected, it will be reported as an Academic Integrity Violation at Level 3 or Level 4. The instructor (or content owner) may also independently take legal action against you under Copyright Law.  Simply stated: do not upload any course materials/content to any unauthorized site without the express written permission of the instructor/copyright holder.
Citing G-AI tools:
In all cases, the specific use of a G-AI tool must be properly and completely cited as follows:
•	Citing routine use of a built-in G-AI tool to correct individual errors for grammar, typos, clarification, etc., use the following format with only one citation for the entire document.
<Company name)>, <Name of the tool>. Accessed on <date in which you          used the tool>, Model or Version: <model or version used>, <descriptor>. Available at:        <link to the main page for the tool>. Context: provide a brief description of the use.
•	Example 1: Grammarly Inc, Grammarly. Accessed on 15 June 2025, Version: 14.1232.0 (browser), large language model-based writing assistant integrated into Word. Available at:  https://www.grammarly.com. Context: used for routine grammar /typo correction.
◦	Example 2: Google, Gemini. Accessed on 20 July 2025, Model: Gemini 2.0 Flash, large language model-based writing assistant integrated into Google Docs. Available at: https://gemini.google.com/app. Context: used for routine correction for grammar and typos, and obtaining a more concise writing.
•	For all other and more substantial uses of G-AI tools, use the following format, and include a separate citation for each use. If you are using up to three prompts, include all. For longer conversations, include the first, second, and last prompt with ellipses (...) in between.  For additional clarification, when needed, provide context. If asked by the faculty, include the entire transcript as an appendix.

The policy, which was jointly issued by the Division of Information Resources & Technology and the Office of the Provost, states:

You will be asked to explain your code and demonstrate your understanding, and thereby prove that it is your own work.
•	Routine proof-reading for correcting grammar, typos, clarifying or correcting sentences, so long as the original sentences are yours.
•	Generating non-technical figures to be used as concept illustrations (subject to course-specific permissions - check with the course instructor)
•	Any assignment or exercise where the instructor specifically and explicitly asks you to use an AI tool for a specific task or purpose that is aligned with course objectives and/or outcomes.

text:
Rowan University recently adopted a new Artificial Intelligence (AI) Policy that establishes rules around how institutional data may be used in tools like ChatGPT.
The policy, which was jointly issued by the Division of Information Resources & Technology and the Office of the Provost, states:
1	Only Rowan data classified as public may be used in non-approved AI tools. 
2	Data of any classification type other than public may only be used in approved AI tools.


Appropriate and acceptable use of G-AI tools includes the following:
•	Research or learn something new, and/or help your own learning and understanding of any topic.
•	Idea brainstorming for projects, proposals, discussion points, etc.
•	Literature searches to suggest papers or summarize academic content; however, literature review and final citations must always be your synthesis of the reviewed content, and be confirmed from verifiable and reputable sources (e.g., Google Scholar, IEEE, arXiv).
•	For starting or creating a general/routine structure for coding, and/or debugging your code, so long as the substantial/vast majority (75% or higher, not counting the documentation part) of the code is yours, and that *you* understand, test, and document the code entirely and thoroughly. You will be asked to explain your code and demonstrate your understanding, and thereby prove that it is your own work.
•	Routine proof-reading for correcting grammar, typos, clarifying or correcting sentences, so long as the original sentences are yours.
•	Generating non-technical figures to be used as concept illustrations (subject to course-specific permissions - check with the course instructor)
•	Any assignment or exercise where the instructor specifically and explicitly asks you to use an AI tool for a specific task or purpose that is aligned with course objectives and/or outcomes.
Use of G-AI tools for any of the following is inappropriate and not allowed:
The following is a set of examples and not an exhaustive list. Some overlap and repetition among the following items is deliberate and intended for reinforcement. If you are unsure whether a particular G-AI use case is appropriate, please reach out to your course professor.
•	Any use of a G-AI tool that is not properly and thoroughly cited (see below for guidelines on how to cite AI-generated content).
•	Solving or answering any questions in any graded assignment, quiz, exam, or report.
•	Analyzing data, drawing conclusions based on experiments or data analysis to be used in any graded assignment.
•	Answering any essay-type questions (other than for language clarification as indicated above) in any graded assignment, quiz, exam, or report.
•	Determining impact factors, ethical and professional considerations for any design-related course (including Embedded Systems, Engineering Clinics, Professionalism & Consulting, Frontiers in Engineering) that asks you to articulate your design decisions, professional judgment, and ethical discussions in consideration of impact factors. 
•	Code or code fragments that exceed 25% of the total script for any programming assignment or any project that requires you to develop code. If the instructor provides you with a base code to modify or to add to, then the modifications or additions cannot be AI-generated and must all be your work.
•	Uploading class/course material, lecture notes to any unauthorized G-AI tool (e.g., ChatGPT and others), or online learning platform (including Chegg, CourseHero, and other similar platforms).
•	Mathematical derivations submitted as part of a graded assignment, quiz, exam, or report.
•	Algorithm design submitted as part of a graded assignment, quiz, exam, or report.
•	Using AI to generate any part or section of a lab report, project report, or any other submission. For example, uploading raw data, results, or incomplete notes into AI to generate a report is not permitted.
•	Using AI to interpret, process, or analyze results from simulations.
It is worth noting that:
1	Pretending or presenting any content as if it is yours that is, in fact, generated by others (including Gen AI) is plagiarism. Paraphrasing or rewording the borrowed content to hide its original source is not only plagiarism, but also academic dishonesty. Either case is a form of academic integrity violation that will not be tolerated and will be reported to the Provost’s Office in accordance with Rowan University's Academic Integrity Policy.
2	Lecture notes made available to you are the intellectual property of the course developer/instructor. These lecture notes and materials are copyrighted and protected by copyright law, regardless of whether a copyright notice is visible (as is the case for any work of authorship under US law). When provided to you (such as on Canvas), you are merely given the very limited right to use them for your own personal learning. Therefore, uploading any course content to any online portal, including online learning platforms such as Course Hero, Chegg, etc., or any Gen AI platforms (such as ChatGPT, CoPilot, Gemini, etc.) is illegal and strictly prohibited. If detected, it will be reported as an Academic Integrity Violation at Level 3 or Level 4. The instructor (or content owner) may also independently take legal action against you under Copyright Law.  Simply stated: do not upload any course materials/content to any unauthorized site without the express written permission of the instructor/copyright holder.
Citing G-AI tools:
In all cases, the specific use of a G-AI tool must be properly and completely cited as follows:
•	Citing routine use of a built-in G-AI tool to correct individual errors for grammar, typos, clarification, etc., use the following format with only one citation for the entire document.
<Company name)>, <Name of the tool>. Accessed on <date in which you          used the tool>, Model or Version: <model or version used>, <descriptor>. Available at:        <link to the main page for the tool>. Context: provide a brief description of the use.
•	Example 1: Grammarly Inc, Grammarly. Accessed on 15 June 2025, Version: 14.1232.0 (browser), large language model-based writing assistant integrated into Word. Available at:  https://www.grammarly.com. Context: used for routine grammar /typo correction.
◦	Example 2: Google, Gemini. Accessed on 20 July 2025, Model: Gemini 2.0 Flash, large language model-based writing assistant integrated into Google Docs. Available at: https://gemini.google.com/app. Context: used for routine correction for grammar and typos, and obtaining a more concise writing.
•	For all other and more substantial uses of G-AI tools, use the following format, and include a separate citation for each use. If you are using up to three prompts, include all. For longer conversations, include the first, second, and last prompt with ellipses (...) in between.  For additional clarification, when needed, provide context. If asked by the faculty, include the entire transcript as an appendix.

Available at: <link to the main page for the tool>.  (if applicable, Context: provide a brief explanation), (If applicable, add: complete transcript provided in Appendix).
•	Example 1: OpenAI, ChatGPT, “Can you explain the practical meaning of eigenvectors and eigenvalues with examples at a level appropriate for someone who is in the second year of an engineering program?,” Accessed on 1 July 2025. Model GPT-4o, large language model-based AI chatbot. Available at: https://chatgpt.com/

How do I get it to show the actual frequency?” Accessed on 17 June 2025, Model Gemini 2.5 Pro (preview), large language model-based AI chatbot. I’m a second-year ECE student learning embedded programming,” Accessed on 13 June 2025. Model GPT-4o, large language model-based AI chatbot. Available at: https://chatgpt.com/. Guidance on AI

Generative Artificial Intelligence (AI) holds promise in improving higher education, offering both opportunities and challenges for universities. AI-powered tools can provide new learning modes, personalize learning experiences, and enable students to receive tailored support and feedback. Additionally, AI can streamline administrative tasks, enhancing efficiency and potentially reducing operational costs. However, the integration of AI also raises important questions about data privacy, ethics, algorithmic bias, and the need for faculty and staff preparation. Balancing AI’s potential and addressing these challenges is important, as the advent of these tools is already reshaping aspects of higher education.

AI and Academic Integrity
The UHM student code of conduct (IV.B.1.a) addresses “Cheating, plagiarism, or other forms of academic dishonesty.” It gives the instructor authority over defining unauthorized assistance, authorized sources, and specifically prohibited behavior in classes. For this reason, instructors are strongly encouraged to:
	1	Be specific about expectations and limitations on student use of AI in assignments,
	2	Hold students responsible for the accuracy of facts and sources used in assignments, and to
	3	Talk through scenarios with classes to provide clarity on expectations
Syllabi and class discussions should make instructor expectations clear with respect to use of AI tools. UHOIC maintains sample statements for adaptation in a syllabus or specific assignments.

Assignment and Assessment Redesign
The widespread availability of AI tools creates both challenges and opportunities for instructors. Similar to the reframing required at the onset of digital calculators (at least for math and science instruction) and internet search engines, assignments and assessments may need redesign to achieve our learning objectives.

name: Abhipsa Panda
text:
Narrative
Generative AI systems use LLMs that are trained on the content available to the systems. For example, the ChatGPT products offered by OpenAI at no cost largely use information that is available on the public internet. Any data provided to these systems will also be incorporated into the model; this is meant to improve the ability of the AI to respond to questions or prompts.
These guidelines do not intend to discourage the use of technology that contains AI functionality, but to allow for the safe exploration of how these tools can enhance the academic experience or provide efficiencies for administrative tasks. The intent is to ensure that doing so does not have an adverse impact on the confidentiality of university data or the privacy of the entire WSU community.
Several initiatives are being taken at the university already, for example, C&IT is currently testing AI features that have been incorporated into some of the more popular tools used on campus, including Zoom AI companion, Microsoft Copilot, and upcoming enhancements to Canvas. Updates will be provided as they become available.
Many generative AI companies have introduced paid models that provide increased data security and privacy, but not all organizations meet the data protection needs required by the university. Please refer to the list of approved generative AI tools.
Data security and privacy guidelines
AI is a quickly growing and changing technology; some products have incorporated options to not use user-submitted data or allow user-submitted data to be removed from the underlying LLM. While these options may exist, they vary from product to product and should be validated with the vendor before using any generative AI tool. Even if those options are available, you should avoid using any non-publicly available data (e.g., exists in the public WSU website) when using any product that has incorporated generative AI technology.
Examples
•	Any enterprise data that may have been generated from reporting tools (Cognos, Power BI) or directly from enterprise applications (Banner, ODS, STARS), even if you have been granted access to the data.
•	Any data associated with a student that would normally be considered FERPA protected, including grading student assignments or identifying work of a student that may have been generated by AI.
•	Any information containing PII, PHI, financial data, HR data, or research data that has not been fully sanitized or contains a cell size of less than ten.
•	Any information that contains copyrights or trademarks, including those of the University.
•	Any video, audio recordings, or AI-generated transcripts that might contain discussions about sensitive data or have an impact on the privacy of those participating.
AI companions for online meetings
Zoom, Teams, and other online meeting tools now allow for features that will summarize a meeting or provide other helpful features. The tools also use LLMs and require additional consideration.
•	All AI tools must first be approved by C&IT; third-party AI bots are not approved for use at this time. Exceptions must follow the purchasing process for technology purchases.
•	While not always required, these tools are most useful when the meeting is recorded. Before recording a meeting, all policies and guidelines on recording meetings should be followed.
•	Respect the privacy of the individuals in attendance, including those of attendees outside the university who may have different policies or rules that need to be followed.
•	AI is not perfect and often makes mistakes during transcription. For example, when a conference room of several people joins a meeting, attribution for the entire room is given to a single entity. Most tools allow for editing and reviewing of the AI-generated content before publishing; this should always be done by the meeting organizer before publishing the results.
•	WSU cannot control the use of AI with meetings hosted outside by someone outside the University or with technology not provided by C&IT. If joining a meeting hosted by a third-party that is using AI where confidential information may be discussed or you do not feel comfortable with the use of the technology you should first try to negotiate another solution with the meeting organizer if a solution cannot be found consult with your supervisor on the necessity of attending the meeting.
•	If you are hosting a meeting and do not wish to have AI bots join the meeting, the waiting room features should be used to permit attendees and deny AI bots from participating.
Other security risks of AI technology
•	Generative AI is already being used in phishing attacks and online scams. As technology advances, it will become easier to spoof identities and allow for better-crafted messages. These advances make identifying red flags more difficult. For example, messages may contain fewer grammatical errors or unusual phrasing caused by language translation errors. Take extra care to identify other red flags, such as creating a sense of urgency, season messages, or offers that are just too good to be true. Some signs of the use of AI are misusing slang or industry jargon and abnormal abbreviations.
•	Generative AI also extends to images and video. This technology, especially with video, is effective but still maturing. If you suspect you are in a video conference with someone, some signs to look for are artifacts during quick movement or improper display of body parts (i.e. back of someone’s head) are signs AI is being used.
•	Several generative AI tools now offer mobile apps available through Apple or Google app stores. Fake apps that mimic well-known tools or others that are intentionally meant to steal data are becoming more prevalent. Caution should always be taken to only install apps from a trusted source, but the best course of action to avoid data theft from the apps is to follow the guidelines in the document.
If you ever suspect that you have been scammed by any source of technology that has impacted university data or your WSU account, contact the Help Desk immediately.
Purchasing or signing up for accounts to access tools containing AI technology
Per APPM 9.8. technology purchases, including those that are considered to be free or open source, require approval by C&IT. OGC may also need to review legal terms and conditions.
AI components are increasingly being added to existing tools that may have already been purchased and gone through this review. It is important to work with a vendor to identify when these changes take place, as they often come with addenda to existing agreements. These terms may at times come as pop-ups or click-through agreements; please do not agree without review and approval. It is also important to regularly review release notes, which may identify these updates. Those new features and terms should also be reviewed by C&IT and OGC.
If you are interested in purchasing a tool containing AI technology or have a new set of terms for using AI or other enhancements, please contact WSU procurement to start the process.

name: Abhipsa Panda
text:
Narrative
Generative AI systems use LLMs that are trained on the content available to the systems. For example, the ChatGPT products offered by OpenAI at no cost largely use information that is available on the public internet. Any data provided to these systems will also be incorporated into the model; this is meant to improve the ability of the AI to respond to questions or prompts.
These guidelines do not intend to discourage the use of technology that contains AI functionality, but to allow for the safe exploration of how these tools can enhance the academic experience or provide efficiencies for administrative tasks. The intent is to ensure that doing so does not have an adverse impact on the confidentiality of university data or the privacy of the entire WSU community.
Several initiatives are being taken at the university already, for example, C&IT is currently testing AI features that have been incorporated into some of the more popular tools used on campus, including Zoom AI companion, Microsoft Copilot, and upcoming enhancements to Canvas. Updates will be provided as they become available.
Many generative AI companies have introduced paid models that provide increased data security and privacy, but not all organizations meet the data protection needs required by the university. Please refer to the list of approved generative AI tools.
Data security and privacy guidelines
AI is a quickly growing and changing technology; some products have incorporated options to not use user-submitted data or allow user-submitted data to be removed from the underlying LLM. While these options may exist, they vary from product to product and should be validated with the vendor before using any generative AI tool. Even if those options are available, you should avoid using any non-publicly available data (e.g., exists in the public WSU website) when using any product that has incorporated generative AI technology.
Examples
•	Any enterprise data that may have been generated from reporting tools (Cognos, Power BI) or directly from enterprise applications (Banner, ODS, STARS), even if you have been granted access to the data.
•	Any data associated with a student that would normally be considered FERPA protected, including grading student assignments or identifying work of a student that may have been generated by AI.
•	Any information containing PII, PHI, financial data, HR data, or research data that has not been fully sanitized or contains a cell size of less than ten.
•	Any information that contains copyrights or trademarks, including those of the University.
•	Any video, audio recordings, or AI-generated transcripts that might contain discussions about sensitive data or have an impact on the privacy of those participating.
AI companions for online meetings
Zoom, Teams, and other online meeting tools now allow for features that will summarize a meeting or provide other helpful features. The tools also use LLMs and require additional consideration.
•	All AI tools must first be approved by C&IT; third-party AI bots are not approved for use at this time. Exceptions must follow the purchasing process for technology purchases.
•	While not always required, these tools are most useful when the meeting is recorded. Before recording a meeting, all policies and guidelines on recording meetings should be followed.
•	Respect the privacy of the individuals in attendance, including those of attendees outside the university who may have different policies or rules that need to be followed.
•	AI is not perfect and often makes mistakes during transcription. For example, when a conference room of several people joins a meeting, attribution for the entire room is given to a single entity. Most tools allow for editing and reviewing of the AI-generated content before publishing; this should always be done by the meeting organizer before publishing the results.
•	WSU cannot control the use of AI with meetings hosted outside by someone outside the University or with technology not provided by C&IT. If joining a meeting hosted by a third-party that is using AI where confidential information may be discussed or you do not feel comfortable with the use of the technology you should first try to negotiate another solution with the meeting organizer if a solution cannot be found consult with your supervisor on the necessity of attending the meeting.
•	If you are hosting a meeting and do not wish to have AI bots join the meeting, the waiting room features should be used to permit attendees and deny AI bots from participating.
Other security risks of AI technology
•	Generative AI is already being used in phishing attacks and online scams. As technology advances, it will become easier to spoof identities and allow for better-crafted messages. These advances make identifying red flags more difficult. For example, messages may contain fewer grammatical errors or unusual phrasing caused by language translation errors. Take extra care to identify other red flags, such as creating a sense of urgency, season messages, or offers that are just too good to be true. Some signs of the use of AI are misusing slang or industry jargon and abnormal abbreviations.
•	Generative AI also extends to images and video. This technology, especially with video, is effective but still maturing. If you suspect you are in a video conference with someone, some signs to look for are artifacts during quick movement or improper display of body parts (i.e. back of someone’s head) are signs AI is being used.
•	Several generative AI tools now offer mobile apps available through Apple or Google app stores. Fake apps that mimic well-known tools or others that are intentionally meant to steal data are becoming more prevalent. Caution should always be taken to only install apps from a trusted source, but the best course of action to avoid data theft from the apps is to follow the guidelines in the document.
If you ever suspect that you have been scammed by any source of technology that has impacted university data or your WSU account, contact the Help Desk immediately.
Purchasing or signing up for accounts to access tools containing AI technology
Per APPM 9.8. technology purchases, including those that are considered to be free or open source, require approval by C&IT. OGC may also need to review legal terms and conditions.
AI components are increasingly being added to existing tools that may have already been purchased and gone through this review. It is important to work with a vendor to identify when these changes take place, as they often come with addenda to existing agreements. These terms may at times come as pop-ups or click-through agreements; please do not agree without review and approval. It is also important to regularly review release notes, which may identify these updates. Those new features and terms should also be reviewed by C&IT and OGC.
If you are interested in purchasing a tool containing AI technology or have a new set of terms for using AI or other enhancements, please contact WSU procurement to start the process.

name: Abhipsa Panda
text:
Narrative
Generative AI systems use LLMs that are trained on the content available to the systems. For example, the ChatGPT products offered by OpenAI at no cost largely use information that is available on the public internet. Any data provided to these systems will also be incorporated into the model; this is meant to improve the ability of the AI to respond to questions or prompts.
These guidelines do not intend to discourage the use of technology that contains AI functionality, but to allow for the safe exploration of how these tools can enhance the academic experience or provide efficiencies for administrative tasks. The intent is to ensure that doing so does not have an adverse impact on the confidentiality of university data or the privacy of the entire WSU community.
Several initiatives are being taken at the university already, for example, C&IT is currently testing AI features that have been incorporated into some of the more popular tools used on campus, including Zoom AI companion, Microsoft Copilot, and upcoming enhancements to Canvas. Updates will be provided as they become available.
Many generative AI companies have introduced paid models that provide increased data security and privacy, but not all organizations meet the data protection needs required by the university. Please refer to the list of approved generative AI tools.
Data security and privacy guidelines
AI is a quickly growing and changing technology; some products have incorporated options to not use user-submitted data or allow user-submitted data to be removed from the underlying LLM. While these options may exist, they vary from product to product and should be validated with the vendor before using any generative AI tool. Even if those options are available, you should avoid using any non-publicly available data (e.g., exists in the public WSU website) when using any product that has incorporated generative AI technology.
Examples
•	Any enterprise data that may have been generated from reporting tools (Cognos, Power BI) or directly from enterprise applications (Banner, ODS, STARS), even if you have been granted access to the data.
•	Any data associated with a student that would normally be considered FERPA protected, including grading student assignments or identifying work of a student that may have been generated by AI.
•	Any information containing PII, PHI, financial data, HR data, or research data that has not been fully sanitized or contains a cell size of less than ten.
•	Any information that contains copyrights or trademarks, including those of the University.
•	Any video, audio recordings, or AI-generated transcripts that might contain discussions about sensitive data or have an impact on the privacy of those participating.
AI companions for online meetings
Zoom, Teams, and other online meeting tools now allow for features that will summarize a meeting or provide other helpful features. The tools also use LLMs and require additional consideration.
•	All AI tools must first be approved by C&IT; third-party AI bots are not approved for use at this time. Exceptions must follow the purchasing process for technology purchases.
•	While not always required, these tools are most useful when the meeting is recorded. Before recording a meeting, all policies and guidelines on recording meetings should be followed.
•	Respect the privacy of the individuals in attendance, including those of attendees outside the university who may have different policies or rules that need to be followed.
•	AI is not perfect and often makes mistakes during transcription. For example, when a conference room of several people joins a meeting, attribution for the entire room is given to a single entity. Most tools allow for editing and reviewing of the AI-generated content before publishing; this should always be done by the meeting organizer before publishing the results.
•	WSU cannot control the use of AI with meetings hosted outside by someone outside the University or with technology not provided by C&IT. If joining a meeting hosted by a third-party that is using AI where confidential information may be discussed or you do not feel comfortable with the use of the technology you should first try to negotiate another solution with the meeting organizer if a solution cannot be found consult with your supervisor on the necessity of attending the meeting.
•	If you are hosting a meeting and do not wish to have AI bots join the meeting, the waiting room features should be used to permit attendees and deny AI bots from participating.
Other security risks of AI technology
•	Generative AI is already being used in phishing attacks and online scams. As technology advances, it will become easier to spoof identities and allow for better-crafted messages. These advances make identifying red flags more difficult. For example, messages may contain fewer grammatical errors or unusual phrasing caused by language translation errors. Take extra care to identify other red flags, such as creating a sense of urgency, season messages, or offers that are just too good to be true. Some signs of the use of AI are misusing slang or industry jargon and abnormal abbreviations.
•	Generative AI also extends to images and video. This technology, especially with video, is effective but still maturing. If you suspect you are in a video conference with someone, some signs to look for are artifacts during quick movement or improper display of body parts (i.e. back of someone’s head) are signs AI is being used.
•	Several generative AI tools now offer mobile apps available through Apple or Google app stores. Fake apps that mimic well-known tools or others that are intentionally meant to steal data are becoming more prevalent. Caution should always be taken to only install apps from a trusted source, but the best course of action to avoid data theft from the apps is to follow the guidelines in the document.
If you ever suspect that you have been scammed by any source of technology that has impacted university data or your WSU account, contact the Help Desk immediately.
Purchasing or signing up for accounts to access tools containing AI technology
Per APPM 9.8. technology purchases, including those that are considered to be free or open source, require approval by C&IT. OGC may also need to review legal terms and conditions.
AI components are increasingly being added to existing tools that may have already been purchased and gone through this review. It is important to work with a vendor to identify when these changes take place, as they often come with addenda to existing agreements. These terms may at times come as pop-ups or click-through agreements; please do not agree without review and approval. It is also important to regularly review release notes, which may identify these updates. Those new features and terms should also be reviewed by C&IT and OGC.
If you are interested in purchasing a tool containing AI technology or have a new set of terms for using AI or other enhancements, please contact WSU procurement to start the process.

name: Abhipsa Panda
text:
Narrative
Generative AI systems use LLMs that are trained on the content available to the systems. For example, the ChatGPT products offered by OpenAI at no cost largely use information that is available on the public internet. Any data provided to these systems will also be incorporated into the model; this is meant to improve the ability of the AI to respond to questions or prompts.
These guidelines do not intend to discourage the use of technology that contains AI functionality, but to allow for the safe exploration of how these tools can enhance the academic experience or provide efficiencies for administrative tasks. The intent is to ensure that doing so does not have an adverse impact on the confidentiality of university data or the privacy of the entire WSU community.
Several initiatives are being taken at the university already, for example, C&IT is currently testing AI features that have been incorporated into some of the more popular tools used on campus, including Zoom AI companion, Microsoft Copilot, and upcoming enhancements to Canvas. Updates will be provided as they become available.
Many generative AI companies have introduced paid models that provide increased data security and privacy, but not all organizations meet the data protection needs required by the university. Please refer to the list of approved generative AI tools.
Data security and privacy guidelines
AI is a quickly growing and changing technology; some products have incorporated options to not use user-submitted data or allow user-submitted data to be removed from the underlying LLM. While these options may exist, they vary from product to product and should be validated with the vendor before using any generative AI tool. Even if those options are available, you should avoid using any non-publicly available data (e.g., exists in the public WSU website) when using any product that has incorporated generative AI technology.
Examples
•	Any enterprise data that may have been generated from reporting tools (Cognos, Power BI) or directly from enterprise applications (Banner, ODS, STARS), even if you have been granted access to the data.
•	Any data associated with a student that would normally be considered FERPA protected, including grading student assignments or identifying work of a student that may have been generated by AI.
•	Any information containing PII, PHI, financial data, HR data, or research data that has not been fully sanitized or contains a cell size of less than ten.
•	Any information that contains copyrights or trademarks, including those of the University.
•	Any video, audio recordings, or AI-generated transcripts that might contain discussions about sensitive data or have an impact on the privacy of those participating.
AI companions for online meetings
Zoom, Teams, and other online meeting tools now allow for features that will summarize a meeting or provide other helpful features. The tools also use LLMs and require additional consideration.
•	All AI tools must first be approved by C&IT; third-party AI bots are not approved for use at this time. Exceptions must follow the purchasing process for technology purchases.
•	While not always required, these tools are most useful when the meeting is recorded. Before recording a meeting, all policies and guidelines on recording meetings should be followed.
•	Respect the privacy of the individuals in attendance, including those of attendees outside the university who may have different policies or rules that need to be followed.
•	AI is not perfect and often makes mistakes during transcription. For example, when a conference room of several people joins a meeting, attribution for the entire room is given to a single entity. Most tools allow for editing and reviewing of the AI-generated content before publishing; this should always be done by the meeting organizer before publishing the results.
•	WSU cannot control the use of AI with meetings hosted outside by someone outside the University or with technology not provided by C&IT. If joining a meeting hosted by a third-party that is using AI where confidential information may be discussed or you do not feel comfortable with the use of the technology you should first try to negotiate another solution with the meeting organizer if a solution cannot be found consult with your supervisor on the necessity of attending the meeting.
•	If you are hosting a meeting and do not wish to have AI bots join the meeting, the waiting room features should be used to permit attendees and deny AI bots from participating.
Other security risks of AI technology
•	Generative AI is already being used in phishing attacks and online scams. As technology advances, it will become easier to spoof identities and allow for better-crafted messages. These advances make identifying red flags more difficult. For example, messages may contain fewer grammatical errors or unusual phrasing caused by language translation errors. Take extra care to identify other red flags, such as creating a sense of urgency, season messages, or offers that are just too good to be true. Some signs of the use of AI are misusing slang or industry jargon and abnormal abbreviations.
•	Generative AI also extends to images and video. This technology, especially with video, is effective but still maturing. If you suspect you are in a video conference with someone, some signs to look for are artifacts during quick movement or improper display of body parts (i.e. back of someone’s head) are signs AI is being used.
•	Several generative AI tools now offer mobile apps available through Apple or Google app stores. Fake apps that mimic well-known tools or others that are intentionally meant to steal data are becoming more prevalent. Caution should always be taken to only install apps from a trusted source, but the best course of action to avoid data theft from the apps is to follow the guidelines in the document.
If you ever suspect that you have been scammed by any source of technology that has impacted university data or your WSU account, contact the Help Desk immediately.
Purchasing or signing up for accounts to access tools containing AI technology
Per APPM 9.8. technology purchases, including those that are considered to be free or open source, require approval by C&IT. OGC may also need to review legal terms and conditions.
AI components are increasingly being added to existing tools that may have already been purchased and gone through this review. It is important to work with a vendor to identify when these changes take place, as they often come with addenda to existing agreements. These terms may at times come as pop-ups or click-through agreements; please do not agree without review and approval. It is also important to regularly review release notes, which may identify these updates. Those new features and terms should also be reviewed by C&IT and OGC.
If you are interested in purchasing a tool containing AI technology or have a new set of terms for using AI or other enhancements, please contact WSU procurement to start the process.
